newsitem.title: JAPAN: TIFFE Euroyen futures end easier on bond falls.
newsitem.headline: TIFFE Euroyen futures end easier on bond falls.

text.p: Key September three-month Euroyen deposit rate futures closed slightly easier on Friday, weighed down by a drop in yen bond futures late in the session on fears of possible yen bond selling by life insurers, traders said.

"Trade in the Euroyen futures market was subdued until the bond market started falling in the late afternoon. When bond prices slumped, the key September contract fell back to 99.28," said a bank dealer.
The key September Euroyen futures contract settled 0.01 lower at 99.29, traded from 99.27 and 99.32. A total of 35,997 contracts changed hands.
"Despite the late decline, the key contract's floor was solid at 99.27-99.28 as there are no prospects for higher interest rates," said a trust bank dealer.

Long-term bond prices slipped late in the afternoon after chairman of the Life Insurance Association of Japan, Kenjiro Hata, said that some life insurers may sell domestic and foreign bonds and stocks if Tokyo stocks do not recover. The Nikkei stock average ended down 54.30 points at 18,090.04.

During the morning the key September contract rose on lower-than-expected money supply growth in December, traders said. But that rally fizzled as participants grew worried about an early rise in the Nikkei. The Nikkei later retraced.

The Bank of Japan (BOJ) said Japan's broadly defined money supply average of M2 plus certificates of deposit (M2+CDs) grew a preliminary 3.2 percent year-on-year in December, compared with economists' forecasts of 3.2 to 3.5 percent.
Traders said the September contract is likely to ease next week, after failing to hold above resistance at 99.35 during a brief rally on Monday. Initial support is expected at 99.26.

Traders said key events for the market next week will include the start of Japan's parliamentary session on Monday, the U.S. Federal Reserve chairman's Congressional testimony on Tuesday and the BOJ governor's news conference on Wednesday.
"People are anxious to see if the government will propose measures to support the stock market," one dealer said.

The key interbank overnight rate was steady at 0.49 percent with the downside underpinned by banks' repayment of maturing certificates of deposit (CDs). Traders said the banks need short-term funds as large amounts of CDs issued before the year-end would mature on Friday and Monday.
